meta.name: Microsoft Azure Database Administrator Associate DP-300
meta.notes: [new pack: 12 authored DP-300 questions covering deployment, security, monitoring/optimization, automation, and high availability/disaster recovery; answer positions balanced 3/3/3/3] [scheduled-agent]

questions.question: An Azure SQL Database is on the General Purpose service tier with default settings. A developer accidentally truncates a table at 09:42 UTC and asks you to recover the database to its state at 09:35 UTC on the same day. Which recovery option should you use?
options: Restore from a long-term retention (LTR) backup
Use point-in-time restore (PITR) to a new database
questions.explanation: Point-in-time restore uses the automatic full, differential, and transaction-log backups Azure takes within the configured PITR retention window (7-35 days) to restore to any second in time, always to a new database. LTR is for restores beyond the PITR window (weeks/months/years). DBCC CHECKDB REPAIR is for corruption and would actually destroy data. A geo-failover switches to a replica that is continuously replaying the log and offers no per-second rewind, so it cannot reverse the truncate.

questions.question: A new Azure SQL Database must hold up to 75 TB of data, support near-instant database copies and very fast restores, and scale compute and storage independently. Which service tier best matches these requirements?
questions.explanation: Hyperscale separates storage from compute using page servers and a distributed log service. It supports databases up to 100 TB, near-instantaneous database copies and restores via snapshot, and lets you add read-scale replicas and resize compute independently of storage. General Purpose tops out at 4 TB per database and uses remote storage with slower restores. Business Critical uses local SSD and AlwaysOn replicas but is also capped at 4 TB. Basic is a small DTU tier for tiny workloads.

questions.question: Regulators require that credit-card numbers stored in an Azure SQL Database remain encrypted such that even database administrators with sysadmin rights cannot read the plaintext, and that decryption happens only inside the client application. Which feature meets this requirement?
questions.explanation: Always Encrypted holds column encryption keys outside the database (typically in Azure Key Vault) and the client driver encrypts and decrypts data, so the engine and any DBA only ever see ciphertext. TDE encrypts the data and log files at rest, but values are plaintext to any authenticated session, including DBAs. Dynamic Data Masking only obscures result sets for non-privileged readers; the data is still plaintext on disk and to admins. Row-Level Security filters which rows are returned, not how column values are protected.

questions.question: Two Azure SQL Databases are deployed to a primary region and a secondary region for disaster recovery. The application uses a single read/write listener endpoint and must continue working after an automatic regional failover without any connection-string changes. Which feature provides this?
options: Point-in-time restore to a new server
questions.explanation: An auto-failover group on Azure SQL Database provides listener endpoints (a read/write listener and a read-only listener) plus an automatic failover policy across regions, so applications connect to a stable DNS name and continue to work after Azure fails the group over. Plain active geo-replication exposes per-database secondary endpoints and only supports manual failover. Zone redundancy protects within a single region, not across regions. PITR is a backup-restore feature, not a failover mechanism.

questions.question: Users report intermittent slow response from a stored procedure on Azure SQL Database. You need to identify the most expensive queries over the last hour, compare runtime statistics across recent plans, and force a known-good plan if needed - using a built-in feature with no extra extension. Which capability should you use?
options: Extended Events session writing to blob storage
questions.explanation: Query Store is built into Azure SQL Database and is enabled by default. It captures query texts, runtime statistics, and all execution plans, lets you compare plans over time, and supports sp_query_store_force_plan to pin a chosen plan. Extended Events can collect data but provide no plan-comparison UI or plan-forcing. Database Mail is for notifications. SQL Server Profiler is a legacy tool that is not supported against Azure SQL Database.

questions.question: A SaaS workload has 200 small Azure SQL Databases with bursty, unpredictable activity - only a handful are busy at any moment. You want them to share a pool of compute and storage to lower cost while still being billed as a single resource. Which feature fits best?
options: Provision each database in its own dedicated SQL pool
Migrate them to Azure SQL Managed Instance
Use cross-database queries with linked servers
questions.explanation: Elastic pools are designed exactly for this pattern: many databases with low average and unpredictable peak utilization share a fixed set of vCores or DTUs, so you pay for the pool rather than for each database. Dedicated SQL pools are part of Synapse Analytics and are not for OLTP databases. Managed Instance is per-instance, not a shared pool for many small databases. Linked servers add cross-database querying, not resource sharing.

questions.question: You must migrate an on-premises SQL Server database to Azure with minimal code changes. The application depends on SQL Server Agent jobs, cross-database queries, CLR assemblies, and Service Broker. Which Azure database target should you choose?
options: Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Managed Instance is the PaaS option with the highest compatibility with on-premises SQL Server. It supports SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries within the instance, CLR, Service Broker, Database Mail, and most other instance-scoped features. Azure SQL Database (single database) is database-scoped and lacks SQL Agent and cross-database queries. Cosmos DB is a different NoSQL engine. Azure Database for MySQL is a different RDBMS entirely.

questions.question: Compliance requires you to retain weekly full backups of an Azure SQL Database for 7 years, well beyond the maximum 35-day point-in-time restore window. Which feature should you configure?
options: Increase the PITR retention to 7 years
Export a BACPAC nightly to Azure Blob Storage
Enable geo-redundant storage on the database
questions.explanation: Long-term retention lets you keep automatic weekly, monthly, and yearly full backups for up to 10 years on Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, satisfying multi-year compliance requirements. PITR caps at 35 days and cannot be raised higher. BACPAC exports are application-consistent but require manual scheduling and storage management, and a BACPAC is not a transactionally consistent full backup. Geo-redundant storage controls backup placement, not how long backups are kept.

questions.question: You want Azure SQL Database to automatically detect query regressions caused by new execution plans, force the previous good plan, and create or drop indexes based on workload observations - with no scripting on your part. Which capability should you enable?
questions.explanation: Automatic tuning on Azure SQL Database can FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN when a regression is detected, and (when enabled) CREATE_INDEX and DROP_INDEX based on Database Engine recommendations from workload analysis. Resource Governor caps resource consumption for workload groups; it does not change plans or indexes. Database Mail only sends emails. Change Data Capture tracks DML changes for downstream consumers, not query plans.

questions.question: An auditor requires that every successful and failed login, plus every change to server-level permissions, on an Azure SQL Database server be captured into long-term, query-friendly storage so the team can run KQL queries across years of records. Which audit destination should you choose?
options: Azure Blob Storage with append blobs only
The Windows Security event log on the SQL host
A SQL table inside the same audited database
questions.explanation: Azure SQL auditing can write to a Log Analytics workspace, where audit events are queryable with Kusto Query Language (KQL), can be retained for years, and can drive alerts and workbooks. Blob storage is supported but stores opaque .xel files and is not KQL-queryable on its own. There is no Windows Security event log surfaced for the PaaS service. Writing audit data to the audited database itself is not a supported destination and would create a chain-of-custody problem.

questions.question: A reporting application repeatedly runs long SELECT queries against an Azure SQL Database on the Business Critical tier. You want these queries to run on a replica so they do not contend with the OLTP workload, without provisioning any additional database. What should you configure?
options: Enable Change Data Capture and point reports at the CDC tables
Create a separate copy with database copy and refresh it nightly
Add a secondary in an active geo-replication relationship in the same region
Set the ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly connection string to use a built-in read scale-out replica
questions.explanation: Business Critical and Premium tiers include built-in read scale-out: AlwaysOn replicas are already part of the SLA, and connections with ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly are routed to one of those replicas at no extra cost and with no additional database to manage. CDC exposes change tables but does not offload general SELECT workload. A nightly copy is stale by hours. Active geo-replication adds a billed secondary database and is overkill when an in-tier read replica already exists.

questions.question: A production Azure SQL Database currently uses the default Azure-chosen maintenance window, and business owners are reporting unexpected short reconfiguration events during peak trading hours (08:00-17:00 local). You need future planned maintenance to happen outside business hours without changing the service tier. What should you do?
options: Apply a non-default maintenance window such as Weekday 22:00-06:00
Scale up to a higher vCore size and resubmit the request
Open a support ticket each week to delay maintenance
Move the database to the Basic tier
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance support configurable maintenance windows. Selecting a non-default window (for example a weekday or weekend evening slot) tells the platform to perform planned maintenance only during that period, avoiding business hours. Scaling vCores changes performance but not when maintenance happens. Repeated support tickets are not a supported way to defer planned maintenance. Moving to Basic would degrade the service and still subject it to maintenance.
